prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$. Let $A_1$ be the orthogonal projection of $A$ onto $BC$ so that $AA_1$ is an altitude. Let $B_1$ and $C_1$ be the orthogonal projections of $A_1$ onto $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Point $P$ is such that quadrilateral $AB_1PC_1$ is convex and has the same area as triangle $ABC$. Is it possible that $P$ strictly lies in the interior of circle $\Gamma$? Justify your answer.
answer: No. If $D$ is the point of $\Gamma$ diametrically opposite $A$, then $B_1C_1\perp AD$ and $[AB_1DC_1]=\tfrac12\,AD\cdot B_1C_1=[ABC]$, so $P$ must lie on the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $D$.

solutions.title: Find the locus of $P$: the tangent at the antipode of $A$
solutions.body:
Write $\angle A,\angle B,\angle C$ for the angles of the triangle, $R$ for the radius of $\Gamma$, $O$ for its centre, $[\cdot]$ for area, and let $D$ be the point of $\Gamma$ with $AD$ a diameter.

**Positions of $B_1,C_1$.** Since the triangle is acute, $A_1$ lies strictly between $B$ and $C$. In triangle $ABA_1$ the angles at $A$ ($90^\circ-\angle B$) and at $B$ are acute, so the foot $B_1$ of the perpendicular from $A_1$ lies strictly inside segment $AB$; likewise $C_1$ lies strictly inside $AC$.

**Triangle $AB_1C_1$ is similar to triangle $ACB$.** The angles $\angle AB_1A_1$ and $\angle AC_1A_1$ are right, so $B_1,C_1$ lie on the circle with diameter $AA_1$. In the right triangle $AC_1A_1$,
$$AC_1=AA_1\cos\angle A_1AC=AA_1\cos(90^\circ-\angle C)=AA_1\sin\angle C,$$
and similarly $AB_1=AA_1\sin\angle B$. Hence $\dfrac{AB_1}{AC_1}=\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin C}=\dfrac{AC}{AB}$ (law of sines), and the triangles $AB_1C_1$ and $ACB$ share the angle at $A$, so they are similar. In particular $\angle AC_1B_1=\angle B$. Moreover $B_1C_1$ is a chord of the circle of diameter $AA_1$ subtending the angle $\angle A$, so $B_1C_1=AA_1\sin\angle A$.

**$AD\perp B_1C_1$.** As the triangle is acute, $O$ is inside it and $\angle AOC=2\angle B$, so in the isosceles triangle $AOC$ we get $\angle OAC=90^\circ-\angle B$. The ray $AO$ lies inside angle $BAC$, so it meets segment $B_1C_1$ at a point $X$. In triangle $AXC_1$ the angles at $A$ and $C_1$ are $90^\circ-\angle B$ and $\angle B$, so $\angle AXC_1=90^\circ$. Also $X$ is inside triangle $ABC$, hence inside $\Gamma$, so $X$ lies between $A$ and $D$, and $B_1,C_1$ are on opposite sides of line $AD$.

**Area of $AB_1DC_1$.** Splitting along $AD$, and using that $B_1C_1\perp AD$,
$$[AB_1D]+[AC_1D]=\tfrac12\,AD\,(B_1X+XC_1)=\tfrac12\cdot 2R\cdot AA_1\sin\angle A=\tfrac12\,AA_1\cdot BC=[ABC],$$
because $BC=2R\sin\angle A$.

**Where can $P$ be?** In the convex quadrilateral $AB_1PC_1$ the diagonal $B_1C_1$ separates $A$ from $P$, so $[AB_1PC_1]=[AB_1C_1]+[B_1PC_1]$. By the computation above, $[ABC]=[AB_1C_1]+[B_1DC_1]$ (here $D$ is also on the side of $B_1C_1$ opposite to $A$, since $X$ is between $A$ and $D$). So $[AB_1PC_1]=[ABC]$ forces $[B_1PC_1]=[B_1DC_1]$: the points $P$ and $D$ are at the same distance from line $B_1C_1$, on the same side. Hence $P$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $B_1C_1$, i.e. the line through $D$ perpendicular to the diameter $AD$. This is the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $D$, and every point of it is at distance $\ge R$ from $O$.

Therefore $P$ can never lie strictly inside $\Gamma$.

**Answer: No.** ∎

prompt: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. Emerald makes a trip in the coordinate plane, starting off from the origin $(0, 0)$. Each minute she moves one unit up or one unit to the right, restricting herself to the region $|x - y| < 2025$ in the coordinate plane. By the time she visits a point $(x, y)$ she writes down the integer $\lfloor x\alpha + y\beta\rfloor$ on it. It turns out that Emerald wrote each non-negative integer exactly once. Find all the possible pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which such a trip would be possible.
answer: All pairs of positive reals with $\alpha+\beta=2$ (the numbers written must be $0,1,2,\dots$ in order, which forces $\alpha+\beta=2$; then the zigzag path along $y=x$ works).

solutions.title: Show the $k$-th number is $k$, then compare growth rates
solutions.body:
Let $(x_k,y_k)$ be Emerald's position after $k$ minutes and $z_k=\lfloor x_k\alpha+y_k\beta\rfloor$ the number written there. Each move increases $x+y$ by $1$, so $x_k+y_k=k$; in particular the visited points are all different, and since infinitely many integers are written, the trip goes on forever.

**The numbers written are $0,1,2,\dots$ in this order.** The quantity $x_{k+1}\alpha+y_{k+1}\beta$ equals $x_k\alpha+y_k\beta$ plus $\alpha$ or $\beta$, both positive, so $z_{k+1}\ge z_k$. No integer is written twice, hence $z_0<z_1<z_2<\cdots$, and $z_0=\lfloor 0\rfloor=0$. If $z_k=k$ but $z_{k+1}>k+1$, then $k+1$ would never be written (earlier numbers are $\le k$, later ones are $\ge z_{k+1}$). So by induction $z_k=k$ for all $k$.

**Necessity.** $z_k=k$ means $k\le x_k\alpha+y_k\beta<k+1$. Using $x_k+y_k=k$,
$$x_k\alpha+y_k\beta=\frac{(\alpha+\beta)k}{2}+\frac{(x_k-y_k)(\alpha-\beta)}{2},$$
and $|x_k-y_k|<2025$, so
$$\left|k-\frac{(\alpha+\beta)k}{2}\right|<\frac{2025\,|\alpha-\beta|}{2}+1\qquad\text{for all }k\ge0 .$$
The left side is $k\left|1-\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\right|$, which is unbounded unless $\alpha+\beta=2$. Hence $\alpha+\beta=2$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $\alpha+\beta=2$. Then $0<\alpha,\beta<2$, so $|\alpha-\beta|<2$. Suppose $\alpha\ge\beta$ (otherwise exchange the roles of the two directions) and let Emerald move right, up, right, up, …, i.e. $x_k=\lceil k/2\rceil$, $y_k=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$; she stays in $|x-y|\le1<2025$.
- If $k$ is even: $x_k\alpha+y_k\beta=\frac k2(\alpha+\beta)=k$.
- If $k$ is odd: $x_k\alpha+y_k\beta=\frac{k+1}2\alpha+\frac{k-1}2\beta=k+\frac{\alpha-\beta}2$, and $0\le\frac{\alpha-\beta}2<1$.

In both cases $z_k=k$, so every non-negative integer is written exactly once. (If $\beta>\alpha$, move up first: $y_k=\lceil k/2\rceil$, $x_k=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$.)

**Answer:** exactly the pairs of positive reals $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha+\beta=2$. ∎

prompt: Let $P(x)$ be a non-constant polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) \neq 0$. Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ be an infinite sequence of integers such that $P(i - j)$ divides $a_i - a_j$ for all distinct positive integers $i, j$. Prove that the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ must be constant, that is, $a_n$ equals a constant $c$ for all positive integers $n$.
answer: Proof: there are infinitely many primes $p$ with $p\mid P(k)$, $p\nmid k$ for some $k\ge1$; for such $p$ the sequence $a_i \bmod p$ has periods $k$ and $k+p$, hence period $\gcd(k,k+p)=1$, so $a_{i+1}-a_i$ has infinitely many prime divisors and is $0$.

solutions.title: Useful primes and two coprime periods
solutions.body:
Let $c_0=P(0)\ne0$. Call a prime $p$ *useful* if there is a positive integer $k$ with $p\mid P(k)$ and $p\nmid k$.

**Step 1: there are infinitely many useful primes.** Write $P(x)=c_0+xT(x)$ with $T$ an integer polynomial. Then
$$P(c_0x)=c_0\,R(x),\qquad R(x)=1+xT(c_0x),$$
where $R$ has integer coefficients and the same positive degree as $P$. Let $F$ be any finite set of primes and $M$ their product ($M=1$ if $F=\varnothing$). For a positive integer $t$ put $x=c_0Mt$ and $k=c_0x=c_0^2Mt>0$. Since $R$ is non-constant, $|R(x)|>1$ for $t$ large, so $R(x)$ has a prime factor $q$. As $R(x)\equiv1$ modulo every prime dividing $x$, $q\nmid x=c_0Mt$; hence $q\notin F$, $q\nmid c_0$ and $q\nmid k=c_0x$. But $q\mid c_0R(x)=P(k)$. So $q$ is a useful prime outside $F$. Since $F$ was arbitrary, there are infinitely many useful primes.

**Step 2: every useful prime divides every $a_{i+1}-a_i$.** Let $p$ be useful, with $p\mid P(k)$, $p\nmid k$, $k\ge1$. For every $i\ge1$, $P(k)\mid a_{i+k}-a_i$ (if $P(k)=0$ this means $a_{i+k}=a_i$), so $p\mid a_{i+k}-a_i$. Since $P$ has integer coefficients, $P(k+p)\equiv P(k)\equiv0\pmod p$, and $P(k+p)\mid a_{i+k+p}-a_i$, so also $p\mid a_{i+k+p}-a_i$.

Thus $b_i=a_i\bmod p$ satisfies $b_{i+k}=b_i$ and $b_{i+k+p}=b_i$ for all $i\ge1$. Now $\gcd(k,k+p)=\gcd(k,p)=1$, so by Bézout there are integers $u,v$ with $u(k+p)-vk=1$, and replacing $(u,v)$ by $(u+Nk,\,v+N(k+p))$ for large $N$ we may take $u,v\ge0$. Then for every $i\ge1$,
$$b_{i+1}=b_{i+1+vk}=b_{i+u(k+p)}=b_i ,$$
using the period $k$ $v$ times and the period $k+p$ $u$ times. So $p\mid a_{i+1}-a_i$ for all $i$.

**Step 3.** For each $i$, the integer $a_{i+1}-a_i$ is divisible by infinitely many primes, so it is $0$. Hence the sequence is constant. ∎

prompt:
Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. There are $n$ cells on a circle, and each cell is assigned either $0$ or $1$. There is a rooster on one of these cells, and it repeats the following operation:

- If the rooster is on a cell assigned $0$, it changes the assigned number to $1$ and moves to the next cell counterclockwise.
- If the rooster is on a cell assigned $1$, it changes the assigned number to $0$ and moves to the cell after the next cell counterclockwise.

Prove that the following statement holds after sufficiently many operations:

> If the rooster is on a cell $C$, then the rooster would go around the circle exactly three times, stopping again at $C$. Moreover, every cell would be assigned the same number as it was assigned right before the rooster went around the circle $3$ times.
answer: Proof: unwrap the rooster's position to an increasing integer sequence; eventually, in any three consecutive laps, each cell is stopped on exactly twice and skipped once (such a pattern exists somewhere and propagates to the next cell), which makes the whole process periodic with period three laps.

solutions.title: Unwrap the circle and track stops lap by lap
solutions.body:
**Unwrapping.** Number the cells $0,1,\dots,n-1$ counterclockwise and let the rooster start on cell $s$. Record its position as an integer that grows by $1$ or $2$ at each operation (we do not reduce mod $n$): positions $s=N_0<N_1<N_2<\cdots$, where position $N$ is on cell $N \bmod n$. Positions $N$ and $N+n$ are the same cell in consecutive laps. For an integer $N\ge s$ let $S(N)=1$ if $N$ is one of the $N_j$ (the rooster *stops* at $N$) and $S(N)=0$ otherwise (it *bypasses* $N$). Let $V(N)$ be the number on cell $N\bmod n$ at the moment the rooster first reaches a position $\ge N$; if $S(N)=1$ this is the number on the cell when the rooster stands at $N$.

Because positions strictly increase, the visits to cell $N\bmod n$ before the rooster reaches a position $\ge N+n$ are those before it reaches $N$, plus possibly the visit at $N$ itself. Each visit flips the cell, so
$$V(N+n)\equiv V(N)+S(N)\pmod 2. \tag{1}$$
The rules of motion give, for $N\ge s$:
$$S(N)=0\ \Rightarrow\ S(N+1)=1,\tag{2}$$
$$S(N)=1\ \Rightarrow\ S(N+1)=1-V(N),\tag{3}$$
(the rooster never jumps more than $2$; standing at $N$ it moves to $N+1$ if the cell shows $0$ and jumps over $N+1$ if it shows $1$).

**Fact A: no cell is bypassed in two consecutive laps.** Let $N>s$ with $S(N)=0$. The rooster jumped over $N$, so it stood at $N-1$ on a cell showing $1$ and changed it to $0$; by (1), $V(N-1+n)=0$. If $S(N-1+n)=1$, then $S(N+n)=1$ by (3); if $S(N-1+n)=0$, then $S(N+n)=1$ by (2). So $S(N+n)=1$.

Let $W(N)=S(N)+S(N+n)+S(N+2n)$, the number of stops at one cell in three consecutive laps.

**Fact B: if $W(N)=2$ then $W(N+1)=2$.** Exactly one of $N,N+n,N+2n$ is bypassed, say $N+jn$; by (2), $S(N+jn+1)=1$. The other two, $N+an$ and $N+bn$ with $a<b$, are stops. By (1),
$$V(N+bn)-V(N+an)\equiv S(N+an)+\dots+S(N+(b-1)n)\pmod 2 .$$
If $b=a+1$ the right side is $S(N+an)=1$; if $b=a+2$ (then $a=0$, $j=1$) it is $S(N)+S(N+n)=1+0=1$. So $V(N+an)\ne V(N+bn)$, and by (3) exactly one of $S(N+an+1)$, $S(N+bn+1)$ equals $1$. Hence $W(N+1)=1+1=2$.

**Fact C: $W(N^*)=2$ for some $N^*$.** Fix $N_1>s$ and let $x_k=S(N_1+kn)$ for $k\ge0$. By Fact A the sequence $(x_k)$ has no two consecutive zeros, so each window $(x_k,x_{k+1},x_{k+2})$ has sum $2$, $3$, or $1$, and sum $1$ only for $(0,1,0)$. If some window is $(0,1,0)$, then $x_{k+3}=1$ by Fact A and the next window $(1,0,1)$ has sum $2$. Otherwise, if no window has sum $2$, all $x_k=1$. Then by (1), $V(N_1+kn)$ alternates as $k$ increases, and by (3) so does $S(N_1+1+kn)=1-V(N_1+kn)$. Choosing $k$ with $S(N_1+1+kn)=1$ gives the window $(1,0,1)$, i.e. $W(N_1+1+kn)=2$.

By Facts B and C, $W(N)=2$ for all $N\ge N^*$.

**Periodicity.** For $N\ge N^*$,
$$S(N+3n)=W(N+n)-S(N+n)-S(N+2n)=2-\bigl(W(N)-S(N)\bigr)=S(N),$$
and by (1) applied three times, $V(N+3n)\equiv V(N)+W(N)\equiv V(N)\pmod2$, so $V(N+3n)=V(N)$.

**Conclusion.** After sufficiently many operations the rooster's position $N$ is $\ge N^*$. Let it stand at $N$, on cell $C$. Then $S(N)=1$, so $S(N+3n)=1$: the rooster later stands at position $N+3n$, i.e. on $C$ again after going around the circle exactly three times. When the rooster stands at $N$, each cell shows $V(M)$, where $M$ is the unique position in $[N,N+n-1]$ on that cell (no visit to that cell happens at positions in $[N,M)$). Likewise, when it stands at $N+3n$, that cell shows $V(M+3n)=V(M)$. So every cell shows the same number as before the three laps. ∎

prompt:
Consider an infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \dots$ of positive integers such that
$$100!\,(a_m + a_{m+1} + \cdots + a_n)\quad\text{is a multiple of}\quad a_{n-m+1}\,a_{n+m}$$
for all positive integers $m, n$ such that $m \le n$.

Prove that the sequence is either bounded or linear.

*Observation:* A sequence of positive integers is *bounded* if there exists a constant $N$ such that $a_n < N$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$. A sequence is *linear* if $a_n = n \cdot a_1$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$.
answer: Proof: with $c=100!$ derive $a_{m+n}\mid c(a_m+a_n)$ and $a_{m-n}\mid c(a_m-a_n)$, so $\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_n)\mid c(a_{m+n}-a_m-a_n)$. If some $\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_n)>c^2(a_m+a_n)$, this forces additivity along progressions and then $a_k=ka_1$; otherwise a large prime power divides all big terms and hence (after removing a common factor) every term, a contradiction unless the sequence is bounded.

solutions.title: Reduce to two divisibilities, then split on a large lcm
solutions.body:
Let $c=100!$.

**Step 1: two consequences of the hypothesis.** We use only that each of the two factors $a_{n-m+1}$ and $a_{n+m}$ divides $c(a_m+\dots+a_n)$.

*(I) $a_{m+n}\mid c(a_m+a_n)$ for all $m,n\ge1$.* By symmetry let $m\le n$. The hypothesis gives $a_{m+n}\mid c(a_m+\dots+a_n)$. If $n\ge m+2$, applying it to $(m+1,n-1)$ (same index sum) gives $a_{m+n}\mid c(a_{m+1}+\dots+a_{n-1})$; subtracting gives the claim. If $n=m+1$ the claim is the hypothesis itself, and if $n=m$ then $a_{2m}\mid ca_m\mid 2ca_m$.

*(II) $a_{m-n}\mid c(a_m-a_n)$ for all $m>n\ge1$.* Applying the hypothesis to $(n+1,m)$ and to $(n,m-1)$ gives $a_{m-n}\mid c(a_{n+1}+\dots+a_m)$ and $a_{m-n}\mid c(a_n+\dots+a_{m-1})$; subtract.

From now on we use only (I) and (II). They remain true if every term is divided by a common divisor, and this does not affect being bounded or linear. So we may assume that **no integer $D>1$ divides all terms.**

*(III) For all $m,n$: $\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_n)\mid c(a_{m+n}-a_m-a_n)$ and $a_{m+n}\le c(a_m+a_n)$.* By (II) for the indices $m+n>n$, $a_m\mid c(a_{m+n}-a_n)$, hence $a_m\mid c(a_{m+n}-a_n)-ca_m$. In the same way $a_n$ divides this number. The inequality follows from (I).

Call a pair $\{m,n\}$ **good** if $\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_n)>c^2(a_m+a_n)$. (Then $m\ne n$, since $\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_m)=a_m$.)

**Lemma 1.** If $\{m,n\}$ is good, then $a_{m+n}=a_m+a_n$ and $\{m,m+n\}$ is good.

*Proof.* Let $L=\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_n)$. Then $0<c(a_m+a_n)<L$ and $0<ca_{m+n}\le c^2(a_m+a_n)<L$, and by (III) $L$ divides their difference, so $a_{m+n}=a_m+a_n$. Next, $\gcd(a_m,a_{m+n})=\gcd(a_m,a_m+a_n)=\gcd(a_m,a_n)$, so
$$\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_{m+n})=\frac{a_{m+n}}{a_n}\,L>\frac{c^2(a_m+a_n)^2}{a_n}=c^2\Big(\frac{a_m^2}{a_n}+2a_m+a_n\Big)>c^2(a_m+a_{m+n}).\qquad\square$$

**Lemma 2.** If $\{m,n\}$ is good and $d=\gcd(m,n)$, then $a_{jd}=j\,a_d$ for all $j\ge1$.

*Proof.* Applying Lemma 1 repeatedly (to $\{m,n\},\{m,m+n\},\{m,2m+n\},\dots$, and symmetrically with $n$), $a_{km+n}=a_n+ka_m$ and $a_{m+kn}=a_m+ka_n$ for all $k\ge0$. The index $n+(n+1)m$ equals $m+(m+1)n$, so $a_n+(n+1)a_m=a_m+(m+1)a_n$, i.e. $na_m=ma_n$. Write $m=dm'$, $n=dn'$ with $\gcd(m',n')=1$; then $n'a_m=m'a_n$, so $m'\mid a_m$, say $a_m=tm'$, and $a_n=tn'$. Hence
$$a_{km+n}=\tfrac td(km+n),\qquad a_{m+kn}=\tfrac td(m+kn)\qquad(k\ge0).$$
Fix $j\ge1$. By Bézout there are integers $u,v$ with $um-vn=jd$; then $R=u+Qn$, $S=v+Qm$ also satisfy $Rm-Sn=jd$, and for large $Q$ they are $\ge0$ and as large as we like. Put $x=n+(R+1)m$ and $y=m+(S+1)n$, so $x-y=jd$, $a_x=\frac tdx$ and $a_y=\frac tdy=a_x-tj$. By (I) for the indices $y$ and $jd$:
$$a_x\mid c(a_y+a_{jd})=ca_x+c(a_{jd}-tj),\quad\text{so}\quad a_x\mid c(a_{jd}-tj).$$
As $Q\to\infty$, $a_x=\frac tdx\to\infty$ while $c(a_{jd}-tj)$ is fixed, so $a_{jd}=tj$. For $j=1$ this gives $a_d=t$, so $a_{jd}=ja_d$. $\square$

**Case 1: some pair $\{m,n\}$ is good.** Let $d=\gcd(m,n)$; by Lemma 2, $a_{jd}=ja_d$. For $j\ge2$, (I) for the indices $1$ and $jd-1$ gives $ja_d=a_{jd}\mid c(a_1+a_{jd-1})$, so $a_{jd-1}\ge ja_d/c-a_1$, which is unbounded in $j$. Choose $j\ge2$ with $a_{jd-1}>2c^2a_d$, and then a prime $p>\max(2c^2,\,a_{jd-1},\,jd)$. Now $a_{pd}=pa_d$ is divisible by $p$ while $a_{jd-1}$ is not, so
$$\operatorname{lcm}(a_{pd},a_{jd-1})\ge\operatorname{lcm}(p,a_{jd-1})=p\,a_{jd-1}=\tfrac12pa_{jd-1}+\tfrac12pa_{jd-1}>c^2pa_d+c^2a_{jd-1}=c^2(a_{pd}+a_{jd-1}).$$
So $\{pd,jd-1\}$ is good. Its gcd is $1$, because $\gcd(d,jd-1)=1$ and $p\nmid jd-1$ (as $p>jd$). Lemma 2 with $d=1$ gives $a_k=ka_1$ for all $k$: the sequence is linear.

**Case 2: no pair is good,** i.e. $\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_n)\le c^2(a_m+a_n)$ for all $m,n$. Put $K=2c^2$. If $a_m\le a_n$, then $\operatorname{lcm}(a_m,a_n)=a_n\cdot\frac{a_m}{\gcd(a_m,a_n)}\le 2c^2a_n$, so
$$a_m\le a_n\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{a_m}{\gcd(a_m,a_n)}\le K. \tag{$*$}$$
Suppose the sequence is unbounded. If every prime power dividing some term were $\le K^2$, every term would divide $\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,K^2)$, which is bounded. So some term $a_m$ is divisible by a prime power $p^f>K^2$. Let $e$ be the least integer with $p^e>K$.

*Every term $a_n\ge a_m$ is divisible by $p^e$.* If $v_p(a_n)\ge f$ this holds because $f\ge e$. Otherwise $v_p(\gcd(a_m,a_n))=v_p(a_n)$, so $p^{\,f-v_p(a_n)}$ divides $a_m/\gcd(a_m,a_n)\le K$ by $(*)$. Then $p^{v_p(a_n)}\ge p^f/K>K$, so $v_p(a_n)\ge e$.

Now fix any $k\ge1$. Since the sequence is unbounded, there is $n>k$ with $a_n>c(a_m+a_k)$. By (I) for the indices $n-k$ and $k$, $a_n\mid c(a_{n-k}+a_k)$, so $c(a_{n-k}+a_k)\ge a_n>c(a_m+a_k)$ and $a_{n-k}>a_m$. Hence $p^e$ divides both $a_n$ and $a_{n-k}$, and from $p^e\mid a_n\mid c(a_{n-k}+a_k)$ we get $p^e\mid ca_k$. Since $p^{v_p(c)}\le c<K<p^e$, we have $v_p(c)<e$, so $p\mid a_k$. Thus $p$ divides every term, contradicting our normalisation. Hence in Case 2 the sequence is bounded.

So the sequence is bounded or linear. ∎
